source.title: Tracing the Thought of a Grandmaster-level Chess-Playing Transformer
source.authors: Rui Lin; Zhenyu Jin; Guan-Chen Zhou; Xuyang Ge; Wentao Shu; Jiaxing Wu; Junxuan Wang; Zheng-Fu He; Junping Zhang; Xi-Peng Qiu

page_placements.theme: Cross-layer feature persistence, drift and redundancy

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse replacement-layer feature analysis to LC0, a chess transformer, and reports feature validation and cross-layer geometric results bearing on superposition and dictionary-recoverable features; it does not reproduce the original toy-model experiments.
record.gate_note: Excluded case-specific chess interventions, policy-path metrics, and cited findings because they do not measure the claim versions. The paper describes its sparse feature representations as intrinsically one-dimensional, but that is a design choice rather than a comparison of feature dimensionalities.
record.test_reason: The study trains Transcoders and Lorsas on LC0 BT4, a chess transformer rather than an LLM. It reports that dictionary features are rated more interpretable than MLP neurons (Table 1) and that selected features match chess concepts with high precision (Table 2). These results bear on V4 in a new setting. The main contribution, reasoning pathways, uses the dictionaries as a tool. The cross-layer cosine result measures a different construct from V1.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors claim the first sparse decomposition of both MLP and attention in a full transformer (LC0 BT4). They say reasoning pathways expose verifiable tactical logic, including cross-layer superposition of bishop-control features. Quantitative metrics show parallel, largely disjoint pathways that converge on move squares. Limitations: one architecture, coarse rules (splitting or absorption), uninterpretable features, and a hard auto-interpretation task.
record.recipe_differences: Uses Transcoders for MLPs and Lorsas for attention in LC0, rather than reproducing the original toy-network setup or its sparsity/importance sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: Feature interpretations have substantially varying recall; the authors attribute some low recall to coarse rules, feature splitting, or absorption. The three measured bishop-feature cosine similarities vary from 0.82 to 0.97.

fits_no_version.finding: Three bishop-movement Lorsa features in layers 1, 7 and 8 have decoder cosines of 0.82–0.97 (random 0.17). Ablating one weakly affects output, while α=-2 on each drops Qxh7+ from 28.75% to 0.7%.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Same-function features are redundantly distributed across layers (cross-layer superposition) in a chess transformer.

record.problems: The study analyzes one architecture and selected features. Human interpretability ratings have no reported uncertainty. Rule validation uses manually designed criteria and at most 1000 activation samples per feature; some features have low recall. The cited cross-layer geometry result covers three selected bishop-movement feature pairs, not the full feature population.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows omitted; case-specific interventions and quantitative pathway metrics were left out because they do not measure the claim versions.

untested.parts: No toy models, sparsity sweep, phase transition, near-orthogonality or regular geometry.
Capacity competition and importance-based allocation are not tested.
Alternative origins of polysemanticity are not tested.
No LLMs. There is no measure of how many neurons a feature spans. Only one model (LC0 BT4) and one dictionary configuration (k=30, expansion 16).
Stability, canonicity and completeness across seeds or sizes are not tested. Reconstruction fidelity is reported but not as a test of V5.
Lorsa and Transcoder features are 1-D by construction. The authors only speculate that some uninterpretable features may be high-dimensional.

missing.what: Reconstruction faithfulness: all modules have L2 error ratio below 0.3 and explained variance above 0.6, with lower Lorsa EV in middle layers.
Authors note some features remain uninterpretable (dense features), possibly due to reconstruction error or high dimensionality.

record.verdict_notes: Table 2 is a curated, non-exhaustive feature set, so its precision and recall cannot be generalized to the dictionary. Human ratings have no uncertainty and no feature counts. V4 names LLMs, so the chess transformer is a new setting (T3). Superposition is assumed as motivation throughout.

versions.untested_parts: No toy networks or sparsity-dependent transition are tested. The study does not measure whether features are nearly orthogonal across the representation, or establish regular geometry across sparsity and importance settings.
Feature competition for limited capacity, dedicated dimensions for important features, and sharing by less important features are not tested.
The study does not test whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
No LLMs are studied; the model is a chess transformer. The study does not measure the fraction of features distributed across neurons or compare feature recovery across model families.
The study does not test whether dictionary features are complete, stable, or canonical units.
The decomposition represents features as one-dimensional by construction; the study does not compare one-dimensional and multidimensional feature hypotheses.

rows.operation_detail: Cosine similarity of decoder vectors for bishop-movement Lorsa features after LC0 post-LayerNorm
rows.measure: Cosine similarity
rows.note: The high similarity supports shared cross-layer directionality, but does not establish the near-orthogonal geometry described in V1.
rows.check: V1 concerns toy networks storing more sparse features than dimensions as nearly orthogonal directions. This row is a cosine of 0.82 between decoder vectors of the same-function feature in different layers of a large chess model. That is cross-layer redundancy, not V1's geometry. Move to fits_no_version.
